a: Cancer is a group of diseases in which some of the body's cells grow uncontrollably and can spread to other parts of the body. It can start almost anywhere in the body.

q: What are the main types of cancer treatment?
a: Common treatments include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, hormone therapy, and stem cell transplant. Many people receive a combination.
Immunotherapy helps the immune system fight cancer. Examples include immune checkpoint inhibitors (such as anti-PD-1 drugs), CAR T-cell therapy, and bispecific antibodies.
Targeted therapy uses drugs that act on specific changes in cancer cells, such as EGFR, ALK, HER2 or BRAF. Biomarker testing of the tumor helps determine whether a targeted drug may work.
Biomarker (tumor or genomic) testing looks for genes, proteins or other markers in a tumor that can help guide treatment choices.

The FDA can approve a medicine for a serious condition early, based on a result that is likely to predict a real benefit, such as tumors shrinking. The company must then confirm the benefit in further studies. If it does, the medicine gets full (traditional) approval; if not, the approval for that use can be withdrawn.

q: How can I find a clinical trial?
a: Clinical trials test new treatments. You can search ClinicalTrials.gov or the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and ask your care team whether a trial is right for you.

Not all cancer can be prevented, but the WHO estimates that about 38% of cancers could be. Risk can be reduced by not using tobacco, avoiding or limiting alcohol, staying active, maintaining a healthy weight, protecting skin from the sun, getting vaccinated against HPV and hepatitis B, and following recommended screening.

q: Are there new ways to get screened for cancer?
a: Yes. For cervical cancer, the FDA now allows HPV testing on a vaginal sample you collect yourself, in a clinic (since 2024) or at home with an authorized kit (since 2025). For colorectal cancer, FDA-approved blood tests (the first in 2024) are an option for average-risk adults 45 and older, mainly for people who decline colonoscopy and stool tests. They miss most precancerous polyps, and a positive result needs a follow-up colonoscopy. Ask a clinician which test is right for you.
Staging describes how large a cancer is and how far it has spread. The TNM system (tumor, nodes, metastasis) is widely used; stages generally range from 0 to IV.

q: What are common side effects of treatment?
a: Side effects vary by treatment and can include fatigue, nausea, hair loss, infection risk, nerve problems, and skin changes. Immunotherapy can cause immune-related inflammation of organs. Tell your care team about any new symptoms.
Palliative care focuses on relieving symptoms and improving quality of life at any stage of a serious illness, alongside cancer treatment.
Most cancers are not inherited, but about 5-10% are linked to inherited gene changes such as BRCA1/2 or Lynch syndrome. Genetic counseling can help people with a strong family history.

Cancer organizations offer helplines, support groups and resources for patients and caregivers. In the US, NCI's Contact Center (formerly the Cancer Information Service) answers questions at 1-800-4-CANCER (1-800-422-6237); many countries have national cancer societies.
